displayQuote: An Exclamation Point Is Like Laughing at Your Own Joke

meta.title: Who really said "An Exclamation Point Is Like Laughing at Your Own Joke"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Mark Twain gets the credit, but the line is F. Scott Fitzgerald's — recorded by Sheilah Graham in her 1958 memoir Beloved Infidel.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'An Exclamation Point Is Like Laughing at Your Own Joke'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Twain. Fitzgerald said it to Sheilah Graham, who printed it in Beloved Infidel (1958). Twain's own exclamation-point gripe is a different line.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — actually F. Scott Fitzgerald
answer.sourceLine: Fitzgerald said it to the columnist Sheilah Graham while rewriting a radio script for her, and she printed it in her 1958 memoir Beloved Infidel — the earliest documented appearance Quote Investigator found ↗. Mark Twain did grumble about “whooping exclamation-points” in an essay collected in 1898, but he never wrote this sentence, and QI calls the resemblance only a partial match.

source.excerpt: “Cut out all these exclamation points,” he said. “An exclamation point is like laughing at your own joke.”
trail: 1898 — Twain publishes the collection How to Tell a Story, and Other Essays (Harper & Brothers), whose title essay first appeared in The Youth’s Companion. In it he mocks the comic storyteller who italicises his own punchline and “puts some whooping exclamation-points after it” ↗ — the same target, but not this sentence.
1958 — Sheilah Graham, Fitzgerald’s companion through his last Hollywood years, prints the remark in Beloved Infidel ↗, written with Gerold Frank and published by Henry Holt.
1999 — Jon Winokur’s Advice to Writers anthologises it under Fitzgerald’s name in the punctuation section, with “points” changed to “marks,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
Today — a reworded version circulates under Mark Twain’s name on the big quote sites with no source given ↗.
source.excerptNote: Graham had written a five-minute script for her first radio broadcast and showed it to Fitzgerald. Tired from a day’s work at the studio, he sat down with a pencil and rewrote her copy line by line, correcting her grammar and marking the words to stress — and this was the advice he gave as he worked.

author.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.heading: About F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.bio: Fitzgerald was the chronicler of the Jazz Age, author of This Side of Paradise (1920), The Great Gatsby (1925) and Tender Is the Night (1934). Broke and out of fashion by the late 1930s, he moved to Hollywood to write for the studios and lived his last years with the gossip columnist Sheilah Graham, who found him after his fatal heart attack in December 1940. He was an obsessive line-editor of his own prose and of hers — which is exactly the setting in which this piece of advice was handed over.

misattribution.heading: Who it isn't
misattribution.intro: Two things went wrong on the way to the internet: the wrong author, and then the wrong noun.

items.why: Quote sites run a smoothed-out version — “One should never use exclamation points in writing. It is like laughing at your own joke” — under Twain’s name with no citation attached ↗. No Twain work contains it, and the sentence structure (“One should never…”) is the tell-tale flattening of an anonymous rewrite.

Twain really did attack the exclamation point, in the essay “How to Tell a Story” — the comic storyteller who “puts some whooping exclamation-points after it” ↗. Quote Investigator judges the resemblance only partial: the “laughing at your own joke” comparison is not there.

Advice to Writers reprinted the line correctly under Fitzgerald’s name but swapped “points” for “marks,” as Quote Investigator documents ↗ — which is why the “exclamation mark” form is now the one most often quoted.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented appearance is Sheilah Graham’s 1958 memoir Beloved Infidel, where Fitzgerald says it to her over a radio script: Quote Investigator verified the passage on paper ↗ at pages 197–198.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Twain is the default owner of any crisp, funny line about writing, and in this case the misfiling has a real hook to hang on: he genuinely did despise the exclamation point. In “How to Tell a Story” ↗ he sneers at the comic storyteller who cannot leave his own punchline alone — who italicises it, “puts some whooping exclamation-points after it, and sometimes explains it in a parenthesis.” Same target, same contempt, different sentence.

Fitzgerald’s version is the one that survived because it is a better joke. It turns a punctuation rule into an image of social embarrassment: the writer chuckling at his own gag while the room stays quiet. And it comes from a scene worth picturing — a broke, dying novelist sitting down with a stubby pencil to line-edit his girlfriend’s five-minute radio script.
context.detailsSummary: How solid is the Fitzgerald credit?
detailsBody: It rests on a single first-hand account. Sheilah Graham was in the room, but she published the memory in 1958, almost two decades after Fitzgerald died in 1940 — a gap Quote Investigator flags explicitly ↗ before concluding it is nonetheless reasonable to credit him.

The wording most people quote today has already drifted once. Jon Winokur’s 1999 anthology Advice to Writers reprinted the line under Fitzgerald’s name with “points” changed to “marks,” and that is the form that circulates on writing-advice lists.
context.pull: Twain hated the exclamation point too. He just never put it this way.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the saying is reasonably credited to F. Scott Fitzgerald, quoted in Sheilah Graham's 1958 memoir Beloved Infidel (Henry Holt, chapter 18, pages 197–198, verified on paper), that Jon Winokur's 1999 Advice to Writers changed 'points' to 'marks', and that Mark Twain's 'How to Tell a Story' passage is only a partial thematic match.

Mark Twain's essay 'How to Tell a Story' contains the passage 'he italicizes it, puts some whooping exclamation-points after it, and sometimes explains it in a parenthesis' and does not contain 'laughing at your own joke'.
Beloved Infidel: The Education of a Woman by Sheilah Graham was published by Holt, New York, in 1958; the Internet Archive scan is access-restricted (borrow only).

Sheilah Graham (1904–1988) was a Hollywood gossip columnist, was involved with F. Scott Fitzgerald from July 1937 until his death in 1940 (he died in her West Hollywood apartment), and wrote the 1958 memoir Beloved Infidel with Gerold Frank, published by Henry Holt and Company.

F. Scott Fitzgerald was born 24 September 1896 and died 21 December 1940; he was an American novelist (This Side of Paradise, The Great Gatsby, Tender Is the Night) who moved to Hollywood as a screenwriter and lived with columnist Sheilah Graham, his final companion.

PR Daily attributes 'Cut out all these exclamation points. An exclamation point is like laughing at your own joke.' to F. Scott Fitzgerald, and separately notes Mark Twain's remark about exclamation points.
